Glossary

Every key term in the workshop, in one place

Quick reference for every term we use across the four sessions. Each entry notes where the term is first introduced, so you can jump back to the full explanation.

The Cast — Who’s Involved

API (Application Programming Interface) — a structured way for one piece of software to request data or services from another; an agreed-upon set of rules that lets programs talk to each other without either needing to know how the other works inside. In the restaurant analogy: the waiter. (Session 1, Part 1)

Client — the program making the request: your R script, your browser, an app. In the analogy: you, placing the order. (Session 1)

Server — the computer/program that receives requests, runs the backend logic, and prepares responses. The kitchen. (Session 1)

Database — where the data actually lives; the server queries it to fulfill requests. The fridge. (Session 1)

Endpoint — the specific URL where an API resource can be accessed; the stable part of the URL that doesn’t change from one request to the next (e.g., /v1/forecast). (Session 2, Part 4)

The Conversation — Requests & Responses

Request — the client asking for something. For our purposes, a request is written as a URL. (Session 1)

Response — what the server sends back: data, metadata, and a status code, almost always formatted as JSON. (Session 1)

HTTP (HyperText Transfer Protocol) — the standard set of rules for sending requests and responses across the web. GET, POST, PUT, and DELETE are HTTP’s built-in verbs. (Session 2, Part 1)

HTTP Method — the verb of a request, announcing what kind of action it asks for: GET (read), POST (create), PUT/PATCH (update), DELETE (remove). (Session 2)

GET — the HTTP method for reading data. Parameters travel in the URL; nothing changes on the server. Nearly all data science API work is GET. (Session 2, Part 2)

POST — the HTTP method for sending new data to the server; the data travels in the request body rather than the URL. (Session 2, Part 3)

CRUD — the four fundamental operations: Create (POST), Read (GET), Update (PUT/PATCH), Delete (DELETE). (Session 2, Part 1)

Status Code — a number in every response saying what happened: 2xx success (200 OK), 4xx client-side problem (404 Not Found), 5xx server-side problem (500). (Session 1, Part 6)

Rate Limit — a cap on how many requests you may make in a time window; exceeding it returns status 429 Too Many Requests. (Session 1, Part 6)

The Address — Anatomy of a URL

URL (Uniform Resource Locator) — a web address: a single string that says exactly where a resource lives and how to reach it. For APIs, the URL is the request. (Session 2, Part 4)

Protocol — the first piece of a URL (https://): how to communicate. The s means secure. (Session 2, Part 4)

Base URL — the server’s address (api.open-meteo.com): who to talk to. (Session 2, Part 4)

Query String — everything after the ?: the key-value pairs that customize the request, chained together with &. (Session 2, Part 4)

Query Parameter — one key-value pair inside the query string, like latitude=35.28. (Session 2, Part 4)

API Key — an ID some APIs require as an extra query parameter (or header) to identify who is making the request — like showing a library card. Open-Meteo doesn’t need one. (Session 2, Part 4)

The Data — JSON

JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) — the plain-text format APIs use to send data: human-readable, machine-readable, and language-independent. No JavaScript knowledge required. (Session 1, Part 3)

Key / Value — the fundamental JSON pattern "key": value. The key is the label (always in double quotes); the value is the information — a string, number, boolean, array, or object. (Session 1, Part 3)

Object — a set of key-value pairs wrapped in curly braces { }. (Session 1, Part 3)

Array — an ordered list wrapped in square brackets [ ], like ["egg", "cheese"]. (Session 1, Part 3)

Nesting — an object or array sitting inside another object as a value, like "coordinates": { "lat": 35.28, "lon": -120.66 }. (Session 1, Part 3)

Body / Content — everything the server sends back in a response; the JSON wrapped in the outermost curly braces. (Session 1, Part 5)

Metadata — information about the response rather than the data itself: timestamps, units, generation time. (Session 1, Part 5)

In R

Named List — what a JSON object becomes in R: each key becomes a name, each nested object becomes a list inside the list. (Session 1, Part 3)

Parsing — converting the raw JSON text of a response into R data structures (e.g., with resp_body_json()). (Session 3)

Flattening — turning nested lists into a flat data frame (e.g., with as.data.frame()); nested keys join with periods, so coordinates → lat becomes the column coordinates.lat. (Session 1, Part 3)

httr2 — the R package we use to build and perform requests: request(), req_url_query(), req_perform(), resp_status(), resp_body_json(). (Session 3)
